passages.t: ‘Make haste, O God, to deliver me!’: a short cry, heard before
passages.happening:
This is one of the shortest psalms, five verses of urgent prayer. The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. Of David. To bring remembrance” (verse 1). Then: “Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O LORD, to help me!” (verse 1).

He asks that those who want to hurt him be turned back in shame (verse 2), including those who gloat, “Aha, aha!” (verse 3).

He asks for the opposite for God's people. “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, ‘Let God be magnified!’” (verse 4).

It ends as it began. “But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
If this sounds familiar, it is. Psalm 70 is almost the same as the last five verses of Psalm 40 (40:13-17). The note on Psalm 40 points this out. As with Psalms 14 and 53, a prayer seems to have been kept in two places and used on its own. The changes fit Book Two's habit. Psalm 40 says, “The LORD be magnified!” (Psalm 40:16). Here it is ‘Let God be magnified’.

‘Aha, aha!’ is the laugh of people who enjoy someone else's fall. In a world where your good name before the town mattered a great deal, that kind of mocking cut deep. The prayer asks that the shame they wished on him would turn back on them.

‘To bring remembrance’ also heads Psalm 38. Its meaning is debated. Some link it with the ‘memorial’ part of an offering burned on the altar as a reminder before God. Others take it simply as a psalm asking God to remember the one who prays.

‘Poor and needy’ was a familiar phrase in Israel's prayers. It can mean real poverty. It also names someone with no protector but God.
passages.later:
Jesus told of a widow who kept asking an unjust judge for justice until he gave in. He asked, “Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?” (Luke 18:7). He said, “He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf” (Luke 18:8).

Jesus also said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).
passages.asks:
Some prayers have no time for long words. ‘Hurry, O God, help me’ is a full prayer. You can pray it in an emergency, in a hospital corridor, or in the middle of a sleepless night.

Notice that even this urgent prayer stops to think of others: ‘May all who seek You rejoice.’ When you are in trouble, can you still pray for others who seek God?
